readerJob: Understand selected pivotal AI breakthroughs, why they mattered, what evidence supports them and what they did not prove.
lede: The moments that changed what AI could do—from learned features to AlphaGo and AlphaFold—without the mythology.

intro.title: Start here: what earns the word breakthrough?
intro.bodyHtml:
On 10 March 2016, AlphaGo placed a black stone where professional Go commentators initially thought it did not belong. Much later in the game, the strategic idea behind Move 37 became clearer. The move is often retold as the instant a machine became creative or outgrew humanity. The match proved neither.

Straight Answers About AI owns the short practical lesson that a strange output must be checked rather than admired. This book asks the historical question underneath it: what chain of ideas made a result possible, what did the test establish, and what later work inherited the mechanism?

A moment enters this book only if it introduced a reusable mechanism, removed a real prior constraint, produced an observable change, had a traceable consequence and still has an honest boundary. Each chapter therefore carries the same receipt: before → mechanism → observed change → boundary → consequence → evidence needed for the bigger claim.

This is an argued selection, not a sacred list. Progress did not arrive through lone geniuses or one smooth march forward. It came through people, institutions, datasets, hardware, experiments, corrections and some expensive dead ends.

chapters.title: From a better question to machines that could learn
chapters.bodyHtml:
In 1950, Alan Turing replaced the slippery question “Can machines think?” with an observable test: could a machine’s responses succeed in an imitation game? That reframing did not build a learning system, prove consciousness or settle what intelligence is. It made behaviour discussable and testable. Read Turing’s paper.

The larger engineering change came when multi-layer neural networks became trainable. In the 1986 backpropagation work associated with David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, an output error could be propagated backwards so earlier layers adjusted their contribution. In plain English, the system could learn useful internal features instead of receiving every feature as a human instruction. Read the 1986 Nature paper.

The receipt. Before: layered networks could not be trained effectively enough for broad practical use. Mechanism: propagate error backwards and adjust weights throughout the network. Observed change: networks learned internal representations on studied tasks. Boundary: backpropagation did not solve data, compute, robustness or generalisation. Consequence: it became a central learning engine for later deep networks. Bigger claim: “the network understands” still requires evidence that a training loss cannot supply.

chapters.title: 2012: when learned vision won at scale
chapters.bodyHtml:
Image recognition used to depend heavily on features designed by people. AlexNet combined a large convolutional neural network, more than a million labelled ImageNet examples and GPU training. Its paper reports top-five test error of 15.3 per cent versus 26.2 per cent for the second-best entry in ILSVRC-2012. Read the paper.

The achievement was not “a computer can see like us.” The system learned statistical visual features useful for a defined benchmark. Images outside the training distribution, biased labels and deliberately confusing inputs remained problems.

The receipt. Before: hand-designed features limited progress. Mechanism: convolutional layers learned features from pixels; GPUs made training practical at scale. Observed change: the stated benchmark gap. Boundary: benchmark accuracy was not dependable real-world vision. Consequence: the result made deep convolutional networks a serious practical route for later vision work. Bigger claim: robust general vision requires evidence outside this benchmark.

chapters.title: 2014–2015: generation, attention and much deeper networks
chapters.bodyHtml:
Several reusable ideas arrived close together, but they did different jobs.

Attention. Before: a translation system relied on one fixed-length summary of the source sentence. Mechanism: repeatedly weight the source positions most relevant to the next output. Observed change: improved translation results, especially on longer sentences in the paper’s tests. Boundary: no guarantee of truth or perfect alignment. Consequence: attention became a bridge to later transformer systems. Source.

GANs. Before: generative modelling had fewer effective routes to compelling samples. Mechanism: a generator and discriminator improve through a two-player objective. Observed change: useful generated samples in the reported experiments. Boundary: no consent, provenance, stability or truth guarantee. Consequence: adversarial generation became a major synthetic-media lineage. Source.

Residual networks. Before: adding layers could make deep networks harder to optimise. Mechanism: learn a residual change around a shortcut connection. Observed change: the paper reports successful training of a 152-layer network and strong ImageNet results. Boundary: depth alone does not solve dataset shift. Consequence: residual connections became a standard building block. Source.

The bigger lesson: a breakthrough is often a component, not a complete product. “One paper invented modern AI” is usually a tidy story pasted over a crowded workshop.

chapters.title: 2016: Move 37 and learned search
chapters.bodyHtml:
Go’s possible continuations grow too quickly for practical brute force. AlphaGo did not calculate every future game. A policy network proposed promising moves, a value network estimated who was likely to win from a position, and tree search spent computation on useful continuations. The system learned first from expert games and then through reinforcement-learning self-play. Read the AlphaGo paper.

Google DeepMind’s AlphaGo record describes Move 37 in Game 2 against Lee Sedol as having roughly a one-in-ten-thousand likelihood under the relevant move prediction. That supports “far outside expected play,” not “no human could imagine it.” In Go, everyone can agree whether a move was legal and who won. AlphaGo won the match 4–1. That validates match performance; it does not prove Move 37 alone caused the win, was the only winning move or was globally optimal. Rarity, result and strategic interpretation are separate claims. The commentator account is sourced to DeepMind’s 2026 retrospective.

Lee Sedol’s Game 4 victory, featuring his own highly improbable Move 78, matters too. The complete case includes machine surprise and human counterplay.

The receipt. Before: Go defeated practical exhaustive search. Mechanism: learned proposal and evaluation focused tree search. Observed change: victory over one of the world’s strongest players. Boundary: no proof of consciousness, general intelligence or correctness outside a bounded game. Consequence: AlphaZero later extended self-play reinforcement learning with search across chess, shogi and Go. Bigger claim: transfer to medicine, law or ordinary language requires those domains’ own evidence.

chapters.title: 2017–2021: transformers, diffusion and joined-up media
chapters.bodyHtml:
Transformers. Before: recurrent sequence processing limited parallel training and made long-range relationships harder to carry. Mechanism: tokens attend directly to other tokens without recurrence in the core architecture. Observed change: the 2017 paper reports better translation quality with more parallelisable training. Boundary: no guarantee of truth, grounding, low cost or unlimited context. Consequence: transformers became a core family for later language and multimodal systems. Source.

Diffusion. Before: GANs were a leading but sometimes unstable generative route. Mechanism: add noise gradually, then learn the reverse denoising process. Observed change: strong image-synthesis results in the 2020 paper. Boundary: it did not itself supply text guidance or settle training-data rights. Consequence: denoising became the technical lineage for many later image systems. Source.

CLIP. Before: visual classifiers usually needed target-specific labels. Mechanism: learn matching text and image representations. Observed change: broad zero-shot classification in the reported tests. Boundary: the authors document bias and robustness limits. Consequence: language could guide later visual systems. Source.

Technical possibility and social permission remain different questions.

chapters.title: 2021: AlphaFold2 changes the starting point
chapters.bodyHtml:
Proteins are amino-acid chains whose three-dimensional structures help shape what they can do. Determining a structure experimentally can be difficult. AlphaFold2 made a major advance in protein structure prediction from sequence.

It used evolutionary patterns in multiple-sequence alignments, learned residue-pair relationships, a geometry-aware structure process and confidence estimates. CASP14 supplied an important independent boundary: participants predicted withheld targets and results were compared with experimental structures. Read the Nature paper and CASP14 results.

The receipt. Before: accurate prediction remained unreliable for many proteins. Mechanism: learned evolutionary and pairwise relationships feed a geometry-aware predictor. Observed change: high accuracy for many blind CASP14 targets. Boundary: confidence varies; structure does not establish function, disease mechanism, mutation effect, a drug or experimental confirmation. Consequence: many investigations can begin with a testable predicted structure and confidence. Bigger claim: biological conclusions still need experiments or independent evidence. See the AlphaFold Database limits.

The proper chain is sequence → predicted structure plus confidence → biological hypothesis → experiment, not sequence → truth.

chapters.title: Your turn: is this a breakthrough yet?
chapters.bodyHtml:
A company announces: “Our new system scored 18 per cent higher than our previous model on an internal benchmark. It is now in our paid product. This changes everything.” No method paper, benchmark details, independent comparison or external evaluation is supplied.

The honest verdict is not established as a breakthrough. We have a company-reported improvement and a launch. The old constraint is vague. The reusable mechanism is missing. The comparison is internal. No durable downstream consequence has been observed.

To support the grander claim, ask for the task and benchmark, relevant baselines, reproducible or independent evaluation, evidence that the mechanism transfers beyond that test, and a consequence larger than product availability. This does not prove the system is unimpressive. It shows which parts of the receipt remain blank.

For the next claim, write six lines: before; mechanism; observed change and comparison; boundary; consequence; evidence needed for the bigger claim. Progress becomes easier to respect when you can see exactly where it happened.

chapters.title: Sources, corrections and the next edition
chapters.bodyHtml:
Evidence route. Each chapter links its primary paper or authoritative record at the claim. The complete source set is maintained in the canonical edition record. For deeper explanation of neural networks, transformers and model operation, continue to AI Fundamentals 101. Current launches belong in the NewsStand; people’s full stories belong in LUMINAiRY.

Reviewed through: 24 August 2026. Recheck when a primary paper is corrected or retracted, stronger historical evidence changes attribution, or a proposed new moment meets every selection test. Retrospective interpretation and current database claims are reverified before each public edition.

Corrections: report the chapter, exact claim and strongest primary source at the Library correction desk. Do not include private or confidential material. The Library owner and an independent source reviewer approve factual changes.
